blocks.text: **The problem.** Implement a stack — `push(x)`, `pop()`, `top()` and `empty()` — using only **one queue**. As before, you may only add at the back, remove from the front, look at the front, and ask for the size or whether it's empty. `pop` and `top` are only called on a non-empty stack.

blocks.alt: One queue holding 1, 2, 3. A curved arrow goes from the front back round to the back: dequeue the front item and enqueue it again at the back. This rotation is the only tool needed.

blocks.code: push(1)   push(2)   push(3)   pop() -> 3   top() -> 2   empty() -> false

blocks.text: The last problem used a second queue as a parking space while digging out the newest item. One queue can park items **in itself**: dequeue the front and enqueue it again at the back. This **rotation** — the same move as in hot potato — moves an item from the front to the back without losing it.

Rotate a queue of n items **k** times and the first k items move to the back, in the same order. Rotate it **n** times and it is exactly as it started. Every solution below is built from that one fact.
1. Brute force: rotate at pop time, and again for top

Push enqueues at the back, so the queue keeps items **oldest-first** and the newest is always **last**. To pop, rotate the **n − 1** older items behind it — the newest comes to the front — and dequeue it. `top()` does the same rotation, reads the front, then rotates **once more** so the order is exactly as before.

blocks.alt: Popping from a queue 1, 2, 3. Rotate once: 2, 3, 1. Rotate again: 3, 1, 2, so 3, the newest, is at the front. Dequeue it: the queue is 1, 2, still oldest first.

blocks.text: **push O(1); pop and top O(n); space O(n)** — and no second queue.

`top()` is just "the newest item", so keep it in a variable `topVal`, set on every push. During a pop's rotation, the **last** item rotated is the next-newest — exactly the new top — so pop can update `topVal` as it goes. Now only pop pays O(n).
**push and top O(1); pop O(n); space O(n).**
3. Best solution: rotate at push time

Do the rotating **once, when an item arrives**, and keep the queue **newest-first** forever. Push `x` at the back, then rotate the **n − 1** older items behind it. `x` reaches the front and the rest follow newest-to-oldest — the same order the two-queue solution kept, with half the queues. Pop and top become a plain dequeue and peek.

blocks.alt: Rotating one queue at push time. It holds 3, 2, 1 newest-first. Push 4 at the back: 3, 2, 1, 4. Rotate three times: 3 moves to the back, then 2, then 1. The queue becomes 4, 3, 2, 1, with 4 at the front.

blocks.caption: Each push rotates the older items behind the new one.

blocks.text: **push O(n); pop, top and empty O(1); space O(n) in a single queue.** This is the standard answer to the follow-up "can you do it with one queue?"

rows.approach: Brute force: rotate at pop time, and again for top
rows.timeWhy: `pop` and `top` **rotate the whole queue** to reach the newest item; push is O(1).
`top` reads a **saved variable**; only `pop` still rotates.
Each `push` **rotates the older items** behind the new one, so pop and top are O(1).

blocks.text: The trade-off is the same as with two queues — some operation has to dig through the queue, so pick the one your program calls least. What changed is the **space**: rotation lets one queue do the job two did.

items: **A single item** — the rotation loops run zero times; push then pop must still work.
**top doesn't change anything** — in approach 1, `top, top, pop` must return the same item three times. Forgetting the extra rotation scrambles the order.
**top right after a pop** — `push 1, push 2, pop, top` must give 1.
**Pop until empty, then push again**, and **repeated values** like `push 5, push 5`.
**Queue using one stack** — the reverse trick: pop down to the bottom item using **recursion**, so the call stack is the hidden second stack.
**Reverse the first k elements of a queue** — push the first k onto a stack, pop them back into the queue, then rotate the rest behind them.
**Hot potato / Josephus** — the rotation move on its own, from the "How do we use a queue?" lesson.
**Queue using two stacks** — the next problem, and the most famous of this family.
